title: David Jones and reading bass clef on mellophone
summary: David Jones inspired St. Cyr on mellophone and sax, and played the shell parts by reading bass clef as treble.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Did you have any instruction on that or pick it up yourself?

Well, David Jones inspired me. He was playing when I got on the board. He was playing alto, playing the what you call a mellophone, yeah. And he played almost as much on his mellophone as Louis Armstrong played on the trumpet. He was just that good at it. He learned how to play sax right on the board.
He learned how to play sax right on the board. I'm not sure, I believe he got a few lessons from Norman Mason. And he just went right on from there and became one of our best saxophone players.
I know Armstrong gives him credit for helping him with his music too.

Yeah, he was a very good musician. I think he used to play mellophone and he used to play the shell parts. We always had horn parts in the band. But he never used the horn parts. He played the shell parts.
I see how he had read that bass clef and treated it as if it was transposing an E flat instant.
Well, yeah, he told me how he did it. A lot of guys used to wonder how he did it.
Yeah, he played it just as it was. In other words, it was in the bass clef. But he played it as though as in the treble clef.
Yeah, and then on the E flat instrument it comes out right. It comes out right. That's the other one. Yeah, I never thought of that.
He said a lot of guys were wondering how I'd do it. He explained to me just how it was. He just played it straight just like he was reading treble clef.
